blocks.text: A 71-year-old man is admitted with fever and abdominal pain. His pulse is 118, blood pressure 84/46, his hands are warm and his urine output has fallen to almost nothing. Is this shock, and if so, which kind? The answer decides whether he needs fluid, a vasopressor, a drain or all three.

blocks.markdown: **Shock** is acute circulatory failure in which oxygen delivery to the tissues does not meet metabolic demand. Hypotension is common but not required for the definition; tissues can be starved of oxygen while the blood pressure is still preserved by compensation. Oxygen delivery depends on cardiac output (CO) and arterial oxygen content, and cardiac output depends on heart rate and stroke volume. Blood pressure depends on cardiac output and systemic vascular resistance.

blocks.caption: MAP: mean arterial pressure; CO: cardiac output; SVR: systemic vascular resistance; HR: heart rate; SV: stroke volume. Pressures in mmHg.

blocks.title: Four categories of shock
blocks.text: Hypovolaemic: reduced circulating volume (haemorrhage, fluid loss). Cardiogenic: pump failure (myocardial infarction, arrhythmia, valve failure). Obstructive: blocked flow outside the myocardium (tension pneumothorax, cardiac tamponade, massive pulmonary embolism). Distributive: vasodilatation and maldistribution of flow (sepsis, anaphylaxis, neurogenic shock).

blocks.caption: Typical haemodynamic patterns; mixed pictures are common, and sepsis can include a cardiomyopathy or hypovolaemia

blocks.title: Classifying shock from the bedside
blocks.prompt: A 63-year-old has HR 128, BP 82/44, cold clammy peripheries, a raised JVP, bibasal crackles and a new third heart sound. Which category of shock is this, and why?

steps.text: Look at perfusion: cold, clammy peripheries imply high SVR (vasoconstriction) and low cardiac output, which excludes early distributive shock where peripheries are warm.
Look at filling: a raised JVP means the venous pressure is high, so the heart is not under-filled; this excludes hypovolaemia.

Consider obstruction: no tracheal deviation, muffled heart sounds or evidence of pulmonary embolism are given, whereas crackles and a third heart sound indicate pulmonary congestion from left ventricular failure.

Conclude cardiogenic shock. Fluid would worsen pulmonary oedema, so management focuses on the cause (for example urgent ECG and reperfusion for infarction) and cautious inotropic or vasopressor support in critical care (check local guidance).

blocks.answer: Cardiogenic shock: low output with high SVR and high filling pressures; avoid large fluid boluses.

blocks.markdown: **Anaphylaxis** is a severe, life-threatening systemic hypersensitivity reaction, usually IgE-mediated, in which mast cell mediators cause vasodilatation, capillary leak, bronchospasm and airway swelling. It is a distributive shock with an airway and breathing component. Recognise it by a sudden onset after exposure with Airway and/or Breathing and/or Circulation problems, usually accompanied by skin changes (urticaria, flushing, angioedema). Skin changes can be absent, so do not wait for them.

blocks.title: Immediate treatment of anaphylaxis
blocks.text: Remove the trigger if possible, call for help, lie the patient flat with legs raised (or sit if breathless), and give intramuscular adrenaline into the anterolateral thigh without delay. Give high-flow oxygen, establish IV access and give IV fluid for hypotension. Repeat IM adrenaline after about 5 minutes if there is no improvement. Antihistamines and corticosteroids are not first-line and must never delay adrenaline. Doses: check against current Resuscitation Council UK anaphylaxis guidance.

blocks.title: Checking an adrenaline dose for an adult
blocks.prompt: RCUK anaphylaxis guidance as generally taught gives an adult IM dose of 500 micrograms. The ampoule is labelled 1 mg in 1 mL (1:1000). What volume is drawn up, and why is this safer than guessing?

steps.text: Convert units: 1 mg = 1000 micrograms, so the ampoule contains 1000 micrograms per mL.
Volume needed is dose divided by concentration.

Check route and concentration: the 1 mg/mL (1:1000) preparation is for the IM route. A 0.1 mg/mL (1:10,000) preparation is for IV cardiac arrest use by experienced staff; confusing them is a recognised cause of harm.
Confirm against current RCUK and local guidance, including paediatric age or weight bands, which differ from the adult dose.

blocks.answer: 0.5 mL of 1 mg/mL adrenaline IM into the anterolateral thigh (adult dose; verify against current RCUK/local guidance).

blocks.markdown: **Septic shock.** Sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection (Sepsis-3). **Septic shock** is sepsis with persistent hypotension needing vasopressors to keep the mean arterial pressure (MAP) at or above 65 mmHg and a lactate above 2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid resuscitation. The pathophysiology is vasodilatation, capillary leak and sometimes myocardial depression. Early management follows the Surviving Sepsis Campaign and the UK Sepsis Trust 'Sepsis Six': give oxygen if needed, take blood cultures, give broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, start IV fluids, measure lactate, and monitor urine output, all within the first hour, together with source control.

items: Fluids: an initial crystalloid bolus is standard; the Surviving Sepsis Campaign suggests 30 mL/kg within the first 3 hours for sepsis-induced hypoperfusion (a weak recommendation; check current guidance).
Reassess after every bolus: look for improved perfusion, falling lactate and signs of overload such as new crackles or hypoxia.

Vasopressor: if MAP remains below 65 mmHg despite fluids, start norepinephrine (noradrenaline), the first-line agent in guidelines, ideally via a central line but peripherally in the early phase if necessary; avoid delay.
Escalate to critical care early; further agents are used only under senior guidance.

blocks.title: Fluid then vasopressor reasoning
blocks.prompt: A 90 kg man with pneumonia is hypotensive at 78/40 mmHg after the first bolus. Calculate the 30 mL/kg volume and his MAP, and decide the next step.

steps.text: Volume: 30 mL/kg x 90 kg = 2700 mL of crystalloid over the first hours, given in boluses with reassessment (check current Surviving Sepsis guidance).
MAP = (SBP + 2 x DBP)/3 = (78 + 80)/3 = 52.7 mmHg, which is below the 65 mmHg target.

Give the first bolus and reassess, then continue boluses towards the full 30 mL/kg (2700 mL), reassessing for overload after each. If hypotension persists after the full 30 mL/kg resuscitation, start a vasopressor (norepinephrine) alongside source control and antibiotics rather than giving unlimited fluid. Peripheral noradrenaline may be started earlier if hypotension is severe or fluid is slow, per local policy (check current guidance).
Monitor with an arterial line, hourly urine output and repeat lactate, and call critical care.

blocks.answer: 2700 mL total target volume (reassess as given); MAP about 52.7 mmHg, so continue fluid to the full 30 mL/kg and, if hypotension persists, start norepinephrine to reach MAP of at least 65 mmHg (earlier peripheral noradrenaline per local policy).

blocks.title: Do not confuse the fluid-responsive and fluid-overloaded patient
blocks.text: In cardiogenic shock fluid can precipitate pulmonary oedema, and in septic shock excessive fluid can worsen oxygenation. Titrate to clinical response.

points: Shock is inadequate oxygen delivery; classify as hypovolaemic, cardiogenic, obstructive or distributive using perfusion and filling pressures.
Anaphylaxis is treated first and fastest with IM adrenaline; antihistamines and steroids are adjuncts.
Septic shock management: antibiotics and source control, fluids with reassessment, norepinephrine to MAP of at least 65 mmHg.
Every dose and volume should be checked against current RCUK, NICE, Surviving Sepsis and local guidance.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man vomits a large volume of fresh blood. He is pale and clammy with a pulse of 130, blood pressure 80/50 and flat neck veins. Which type of shock is this?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: blood loss with low filling pressures (flat neck veins) and vasoconstriction.
distractorRationale.b: Cardiogenic shock would show raised filling pressures and pulmonary congestion.
distractorRationale.c: Obstructive shock has a mechanical cause with typically distended neck veins.
distractorRationale.d: Distributive shock gives vasodilatation with warm peripheries.

questions.explanation: Active haemorrhage reduces circulating volume, giving low venous filling, tachycardia and cool vasoconstricted peripheries. This is hypovolaemic shock and needs source control and volume replacement, preferably with blood in major haemorrhage.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old is stabbed in the left chest. He is hypotensive and tachycardic with distended neck veins, muffled heart sounds and clear, equal breath sounds. Which category of shock does this represent?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: raised venous pressure, hypotension and muffled heart sounds after a penetrating injury indicate tamponade, an obstructive cause.
distractorRationale.b: Pure hypovolaemia would give flat neck veins.
distractorRationale.c: Neurogenic shock gives bradycardia and warm peripheries, with flat veins.
distractorRationale.d: Myocardial infarction is not suggested by the history or findings.

questions.explanation: Blood in the pericardial sac compresses the heart and limits filling, so output falls while venous pressure rises. This obstructive picture needs urgent decompression rather than fluid alone.

questions.stem: Which haemodynamic profile best describes early distributive shock such as sepsis?

options.text: Normal or high cardiac output with low systemic vascular resistance
Low cardiac output with high systemic vascular resistance
Low cardiac output with low systemic vascular resistance and high CVP
High cardiac output with high systemic vascular resistance

questions.correctOptionText: Normal or high cardiac output with low systemic vascular resistance

distractorRationale.a: Correct: vasodilatation lowers SVR while the heart compensates with a high output early on.
distractorRationale.b: This is the typical pattern for hypovolaemic and cardiogenic shock.
distractorRationale.c: This mixture does not describe the characteristic profile.
distractorRationale.d: High SVR is not seen in distributive shock.

questions.explanation: In distributive shock, vasodilatation reduces SVR and blood pressure falls despite a normal or high cardiac output. Patients may have warm peripheries early, in contrast with the cold peripheries of other shock types.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old develops lip swelling, stridor, wheeze and a blood pressure of 78/40 minutes after eating a meal containing nuts. What is the single most important immediate drug treatment?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: IM adrenaline is the first-line, life-saving drug.
distractorRationale.b: Antihistamines are second-line and treat skin symptoms only.
distractorRationale.c: Steroids act too slowly and are not first-line.
distractorRationale.d: Bronchodilator alone does not treat airway oedema or shock.

questions.explanation: Adrenaline reverses vasodilatation, bronchospasm and mediator release. It must be given early; second-line drugs must never delay it.

questions.stem: After a first dose of intramuscular adrenaline, a patient with anaphylaxis still has wheeze and a systolic blood pressure of 80 mmHg five minutes later. What is the appropriate next step in line with RCUK guidance as generally taught?

options.text: Repeat the intramuscular adrenaline dose, give oxygen and IV fluids, and call for senior help
Wait 30 minutes to see if he improves
Stop adrenaline and give only steroids

questions.correctOptionText: Repeat the intramuscular adrenaline dose, give oxygen and IV fluids, and call for senior help

distractorRationale.a: Correct: lack of response at about 5 minutes warrants a repeat IM dose with supportive therapy and escalation.
distractorRationale.c: Oral antihistamines are inappropriate in a patient with shock.
distractorRationale.d: Steroids do not treat acute life-threatening features.

questions.explanation: If there is no improvement after the first dose, guidance advises repeating IM adrenaline after about 5 minutes while giving oxygen and fluids. Check current RCUK guidance for exact timing and doses.

questions.stem: A patient with septic shock remains hypotensive after adequate fluid resuscitation. Which statement about vasopressor use is most consistent with Surviving Sepsis guidance?

options.text: Norepinephrine is the first-line vasopressor, titrated to a MAP of at least 65 mmHg
Dopamine is the first-line vasopressor in all patients
Vasopressors should be withheld until 10 L of fluid has been given
Target a MAP of 100 mmHg to ensure organ perfusion

questions.correctOptionText: Norepinephrine is the first-line vasopressor, titrated to a MAP of at least 65 mmHg

distractorRationale.a: Correct: this is the standard guideline approach.
distractorRationale.b: Dopamine is not first-line and carries more arrhythmia risk.
distractorRationale.c: Delaying vasopressors while giving excessive fluid is harmful.
distractorRationale.d: A MAP target of 100 is not recommended.

questions.explanation: Septic vasodilatation requires restoring vascular tone, which fluids alone cannot do. Norepinephrine raises MAP with a favourable safety profile, and a MAP of at least 65 mmHg is the usual initial target; always check current guidance and individualise.

questions.stem: Using the Surviving Sepsis suggestion of 30 mL/kg of crystalloid for sepsis-induced hypoperfusion, calculate the target volume for a patient weighing 68 kg. Give your answer in mL.
questions.explanation: 30 mL/kg x 68 kg = 2040 mL. This is given in boluses with reassessment after each, not as a single uncritical infusion, and should be checked against current guidance.

questions.stem: A patient has a heart rate of 132 beats per minute and a systolic blood pressure of 88 mmHg. Calculate the shock index (heart rate divided by systolic blood pressure). Give your answer as a ratio to one decimal place.
questions.explanation: Shock index = 132 / 88 = 1.5. A ratio well above 1 suggests circulatory compromise, although it is a screening tool and does not identify the type of shock.

questions.stem: Explain the reasoning behind fluid resuscitation followed by vasopressors in septic shock. Include the targets, the risks of excessive fluid and what else must be done in the first hour.
markingGuide: Sepsis causes vasodilatation and capillary leak with relative hypovolaemia, so an initial crystalloid bolus restores preload.
Fluids are given in aliquots with reassessment (suggested 30 mL/kg within 3 hours; check current guidance).
Excess fluid causes pulmonary oedema and worsens oxygenation, so response is monitored.
If MAP remains below 65 mmHg despite fluid, start norepinephrine as first-line vasopressor.
First-hour actions: blood cultures, broad-spectrum antibiotics, lactate, oxygen, urine output monitoring, and source control.
questions.explanation: Fluids correct hypovolaemia while vasopressors correct vasodilatation. Reassessment avoids harm from over-resuscitation.

questions.stem: Describe the immediate management of a 40-year-old woman with suspected anaphylaxis after a wasp sting, including drug, route, site and supportive care. State how doses would be verified.
markingGuide: Recognises anaphylaxis (airway, breathing and/or circulation problem after exposure, often with skin changes) and calls for help.
Gives IM adrenaline into the anterolateral thigh, 500 micrograms for an adult (0.5 mL of 1 mg/mL), early.
Positions the patient (flat with legs raised, or sitting if breathless) and gives high-flow oxygen.
Obtains IV access and gives IV fluid for hypotension.
Repeats IM adrenaline after about 5 minutes if no improvement.
States that antihistamines and steroids are second-line and must not delay adrenaline, and that doses are checked against current RCUK and local guidance.
questions.explanation: Adrenaline is the key drug because it reverses all the life-threatening features. Supportive measures and escalation follow in parallel.
